assessment_summary: The statement claims that any graph in which every vertex-deleted subgraph is Hamiltonian must itself be Hamiltonian. This is false. Graphs with this exact property (every vertex-deleted subgraph is Hamiltonian, but the graph itself is not) are known as hypohamiltonian graphs. The Petersen graph is the smallest such graph and serves as a concrete counterexample.
counterexample: The Petersen graph is a counterexample. Let the vertices of G be the 2-element subsets of {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, with an edge between any two subsets if and only if they are disjoint. This is a finite simple connected graph with 10 vertices. It is a well-known fact that the Petersen graph does not contain a Hamiltonian cycle. However, for any vertex v, G - v has a Hamiltonian cycle. Because the graph is vertex-transitive, we only need to check one vertex. For example, if we remove the vertex {1,2}, the remaining 9 vertices have the following Hamiltonian cycle: {1,3} -> {2,4} -> {3,5} -> {1,4} -> {2,5} -> {3,4} -> {1,5} -> {2,3} -> {4,5} -> {1,3}. All adjacent pairs in this cycle are disjoint sets, meaning they are valid edges in G.
